How can we find the maximum possible value of [MATH: \|A \mathbf x\|?] Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

Graphic:

Content:
First, we note the following:

Content:
- The value of [MATH: \mathbf x] that maximizes [MATH: ||A\mathbf x||] also maximizes [MATH: ||A\mathbf x||^2.]
- If [MATH: \mathbf v] is a column vector, then [MATH: ||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}]

Content:
Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point [MATH: A\mathbf{x}] on our ellipse as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ‖Ax‖^{2}|= (Ax)^{T}(Ax); = (x^{T}A^{T})(Ax); = x^{T}(A^{T}A)x]

Content:
Note that [MATH: \mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}] is a quadratic form with the matrix [MATH: A^T A.] Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for [MATH: \| \mathbf{x} \| =1] equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix [MATH: A^T A.]

Content:
In our case, we have

Content:
[MATH: A^{T}A|= [1|3; − 3|− 1]^{T}[1|3; − 3|− 1]; = [1|− 3; 3|− 1][1|3; − 3|− 1]; = [10|6; 6|10].]

Content:
Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: A^TA\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: |A^{T}A − λI||= 0;|10 − λ|6; 6|10 − λ||= 0; (10 − λ)^{2} − 36|= 0; (10 − λ)^{2}|= 36; 10 − λ|= ± 6; λ|= 4, 16]

Content:
Since the largest eigenvalue of [MATH: A^T A] is [MATH: 16,] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.]

Content:
Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals [MATH: 4.]

Content:

How can we find the maximum possible value of [MATH: \|A \mathbf x\|?] Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

Item 7 — Example: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere Given the Corresponding Singular Values

Example Prompt:
A [MATH: 2 \times 3] matrix [MATH: A] maps the unit sphere [MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}] from [MATH: \mathbb{R}^3] onto an ellipse in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2.] Given that the singular values of [MATH: A] are [MATH: \sigma_1=4,] [MATH: \sigma_2=2,] and [MATH: \sigma_3 = 0,] find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The matrix [MATH: A] maps the unit sphere [MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}] from [MATH: \mathbb{R}^3] onto the ellipse [MATH: \big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}] in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2.]

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point [MATH: A\mathbf{x}] on our ellipse, as follows:

[MATH: ‖Ax‖^{2}|= (Ax)^{T}(Ax); = (x^{T}A^{T})(Ax); = x^{T}(A^{T}A)x,]

where [MATH: \mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}] is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix [MATH: A^T A.]

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when [MATH: \| \mathbf{x} \| =1,] is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix [MATH: A^T A.]

The square roots of the eigenvalues of [MATH: A^T A] are called the singular values of [MATH: A.] Since the largest singular value of [MATH: A] is [MATH: \sigma_1=4,] the largest eigenvalue of [MATH: A^T A] must be [MATH: \lambda_1 = \sigma_1^2=4^2.] So, we obtain that

[MATH: \max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 4^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = 4.]

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is [MATH: \sigma_1=4.]
